q0.answer: Enter a US ticker and it lays out the chart (indicators, candlestick patterns, support and resistance), earnings and valuation, financial statements, recent news flow, options market data, congressional trade disclosures, and short-term buying mood (the Fear & Greed Index) — then an overall conclusion that ties them together. It is free. For KOSPI and KOSDAQ listings it covers chart, earnings, financial statements, news, Fear & Greed and the overall conclusion (Korea has no congressional disclosure regime and no single-stock options market, so those two are omitted). For crypto such as Bitcoin and Ethereum it covers chart, news, Fear & Greed and the overall conclusion. No sign-up needed.
q0.question: What is {v0}?

q1.answer: The Siglens chatbot answers with the chart and indicator data of the ticker you are viewing as context — reading the trend, entry timing, what an indicator means, comparing patterns, discussing strategy. Answers are grounded in the analysis shown on screen.
q1.question: What can I ask the AI chat?

q10.answer: It is free today and needs no sign-up. Advanced features will move to a paid plan later; the core analysis stays free.
q10.question: Is there a fee to use the service?

q11.answer: Major crypto such as Bitcoin (BTCUSD) and Ethereum (ETHUSD) is analyzed like any other ticker. Enter the symbol and you get the 24-hour price chart with indicators, trading signals, the latest crypto news, the Fear & Greed Index, and an AI Overall Conclusion tying them together. For example /BTCUSD.
q11.question: Can it analyze crypto too?

q2.answer: The /market page scans the leading names across 11 sectors every day and lists the tickers where technical signals were caught — golden cross, death cross, RSI divergence, Bollinger squeeze. Click one to open its detailed AI analysis page.
q2.question: What signals does the market overview show?

q3.answer: The Fundamentals tab on a ticker page carries valuation and profitability metrics — PER, PBR, ROE, operating margin — alongside a peer-average comparison. For Apple that is /AAPL/fundamental.
q3.question: Where do I find Earnings metrics like PER or ROE for a ticker?

q4.answer: The News tab on a ticker page gathers recent earnings results, guidance and key events together with news sentiment (the spread of positive, neutral and negative). For Tesla that is /TSLA/news — useful when price moves are not explained by the chart alone.
q4.question: Where do I check earnings and news sentiment?

q5.answer: The Fear & Greed tab on each ticker page (e.g. /AAPL/fear-greed) combines volume flow and price position into a 0–100 score for the short-term mood. Closer to 0 means selling pressure dominates; closer to 100 means buying does. Five labels run from extreme fear to extreme greed.
q5.question: Can I tell whether buying pressure is strong right now?

q6.answer: The market-wide Fear & Greed page (/fear-greed) combines five factors — the S&P 500, VIX, long-dated Treasuries, high-yield versus investment-grade corporates, and the equal-weight index — into a 0–100 score for short-term sentiment across US equities. Where the per-ticker index reads one name’s supply and demand, this page reads whether the market as a whole is overheated or fearful.
q6.question: Where do I see the mood of the whole US market?

q7.answer: The Options tab on each ticker page (e.g. /AAPL/options) shows Max Pain by expiry, the Put/Call ratio, ATM IV, implied move and the open-interest distribution by strike. The AI reads this dense options data back to you and explains which way the market is leaning.
q7.question: Can I see where institutions are betting in the options market?

q8.answer: The Overall tab on a ticker page ties chart, earnings, news, the options market and Fear & Greed into one conclusion — bull and bear scenarios, the key things to check, and the risks. For Nvidia that is /NVDA/overall.
q8.question: Where is the conclusion that combines chart, earnings, news and options?

q9.answer: The /backtesting page publishes two years of technical analysis and AI predictions for major tickers — hit rate and a cumulative-return simulation — so you can judge how much to trust the output.
q9.question: How accurate is the AI analysis in practice?

howTo.step1Text: Type the name or symbol of the ticker into the search box. For example Apple, Tesla, AAPL, TSLA; for Korean listings Samsung Electronics or 005930.KS; for crypto BTCUSD or ETHUSD.
howTo.step2Text: On the ticker page, review the trend and candidate entry zones against {v0} indicators, {v1} candlestick patterns, {v2} chart patterns, {v3} strategies and {v4} support/resistance levels.

howTo.step7Text: When the call is unclear, ask the chatbot directly. With the data of the ticker you are viewing as context, it answers on reading indicators, comparing scenarios and trading strategy.

page.1a9e0a: The U.S. STOCK Act mandates that members of the Senate and House of Representatives and their family members disclose stock trades within 45 days. kr.description: See Korea's economic indicators on one page — policy rate, CPI, employment rate, and GDP growth, plus government bond yields and export growth, along with upcoming release dates.
kr.faq0a: The Bank of Korea’s Monetary Policy Board meets eight times a year to set the base rate. The “Korea policy rate” card on this page shows the most recent decision.
kr.faq0q: Who sets the Korean policy rate?
kr.faq1a: The yield set at auction when the government issues Korean Treasury Bonds. The 3-year is read as the short-end benchmark and the 10-year as the long-end one; a wider gap between them is sometimes read as stronger expectations for expansion.
kr.faq1q: What is the KTB auction yield?
kr.faq2a: It is collected from the Korean release history in the Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) economic calendar. Each card shows that indicator’s latest published value and updates whenever a new release lands.
kr.faq2q: Where does this data come from?
kr.title: Korea Economy — Indicators & Calendar at a Glance

kr.copy_faq0a: It combines recent closes of five factors — KOSPI 200, KOSPI realized volatility, 30-year KTBs, corporate bonds, 10-year KTBs and equal-weight KOSPI 200 — into a 0–100 score for short-term buying sentiment across Korean equities.
kr.copy_faq0q: What does the Korean Fear & Greed Index measure?
kr.copy_faq1a: There is no free quote feed for VKOSPI (the KOSPI 200 volatility index). Instead, 20-day realized volatility (annualized) is computed directly from KOSPI closes and used in its place.
kr.copy_faq1q: Why realized volatility instead of VKOSPI?
kr.copy_faq2a: The formula is the same but the inputs are not. Korea has no liquid high-yield bond market, so the credit factor is proxied by the spread between corporate bonds and 10-year KTBs.
kr.copy_faq2q: Can I compare this score directly with the US index?
kr.copy_faq3a: It updates once per session, on the KOSPI regular-hours closing price. The page itself is cached for up to an hour.
kr.copy_faq3q: How often does the score update?
kr.copy_intro0: The Korean market Fear & Greed Index combines recent closes of KOSPI 200 (KODEX 200), KOSPI realized volatility, 30-year KTBs, corporate bonds, 10-year KTBs and equal-weight KOSPI 200 into a 0–100 score for short-term buying sentiment across Korean equities.
kr.copy_intro1: Each of the five factors is converted to a percentile within its own history, then averaged with equal weights. A lower score means fear dominates; a higher score means greed does.
kr.description: Combining recent moves in KOSPI 200, government bonds, corporate bonds, and an equal-weight ETF, this shows overall Korean market buying sentiment as a 0–100 score with a 5-level label.

us.copy_faq0a: It combines recent closes of five factors — the S&P 500, VIX, long-dated Treasuries, high-yield versus investment-grade corporates, and the equal-weight index — into a 0–100 score for short-term buying sentiment across US equities.
us.copy_faq0q: What does the market Fear & Greed Index measure?
us.copy_faq1a: No. This index is computed independently of CNN, deriving its own five factors — momentum, volatility, safe-haven demand, junk-bond demand and breadth — from daily closing data alone. It leaves out some inputs CNN uses, such as the options put/call ratio, so the direction of fear and greed tends to move similarly while the exact score does not match, because the construction differs.

accruals: It checks how well reported net income is backed by actual operating cash flow.
When operating cash flow exceeds net income (a ratio above 1), earnings quality is considered good.
capex: Money invested in the future — plants, equipment and the like.
Too large relative to revenue is a cash burden; at a sensible level it reads as growth investment.
fcf: Cash left over from the core business after capital expenditure (CapEx), free to use as the company likes.
It funds dividends, buybacks and debt repayment.
Consistently positive means the business generates cash reliably.
fcfMargin: How much free cash flow the company keeps per unit of revenue.
The higher it is, the better revenue converts into cash.
grossMargin: Gross profit — revenue minus cost of sales — as a percentage of revenue.
A higher figure means stronger underlying product profitability.
netDebt: Total debt minus the cash on hand.
A negative figure means cash exceeds debt — a “net cash” position, which is very solid.

page.krDifference: This index is derived independently from daily closes of Korean-listed ETFs and indices. The formula matches the US index, but the inputs differ — do not compare the two scores directly.

callOpenInterest: How many call (upside) options contracts buyers still hold at a given strike.
Heavy call open interest here means many participants have bet that price goes above this level.
When the trend is intact and resistance breaks, it can act like a magnet pulling price higher.
callVolume: The number of call options contracts newly traded today.
High call volume means many are newly betting on calls today — short-term bullish expectations are active.

Read it with OI: volume up with OI up means new money and a strengthening trend; volume up with OI down means positions closing and a weakening trend; low volume against heavy OI means settled bets simply staying put.
maxPain: The price the stock tends to gravitate toward as expiry approaches.
It is where option sellers (mostly institutions) lose the least, so price often drifts there near expiry.
It is not a hard rule — treat it as a reference level.
openInterest: The number of contracts still open (not yet closed) on a given option.
Heavy open interest at one strike means many people have bet on that price.
putCallRatio: Put options volume divided by call options volume.
Above 1 means more puts (downside bets) and a cautious market; below 1 means more calls (upside bets).
At extremes it is often read as a contrarian signal instead.
The bottom sometimes arrives exactly when everyone is afraid.
putOpenInterest: How many put (downside) options contracts buyers still hold at a given strike.
Heavy put open interest here is a pile of insurance bets that price will not fall below this level.
As price approaches, it often behaves like support.
putVolume: The number of put options contracts newly traded today.
High put volume means more new downside bets or hedges today — short-term risk management demand is strong.

Read it with OI: volume up with OI up means new hedges or downside bets arriving as real money; volume up with OI down means positions being closed (hedges lifted); low volume against heavy OI means existing protection is simply being kept.
